title: Big-O Notation
description: Understand how programmers describe algorithm growth, compare implementations, and predict whether code will remain efficient as input size increases.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Big-O notation is a mathematical way to describe how an algorithm grows as the input size becomes larger. Instead of measuring exact execution time in seconds, Big-O focuses on how the number of operations changes relative to the size of the input.

This makes Big-O useful for programming because runtime depends on hardware, operating system load, programming language implementation, and many other details. Growth behavior is more stable. If an algorithm checks every item one by one, it grows differently from an algorithm that repeatedly divides the problem in half.

Programmers use Big-O to predict whether an implementation will remain efficient when it processes thousands, millions, or billions of data items.

sections.title: Why Big-O Matters
sections.content:
Modern applications process massive amounts of data. Search engines process billions of pages, social media systems serve millions of users, navigation software computes routes quickly, and AI systems analyze large datasets.

An algorithm that works well for 10 items can become unusably slow for 10 million items. Big-O gives engineers a formal vocabulary for comparing solutions before those solutions are deployed at scale.
bullets: Compare two implementations that solve the same problem.
Estimate how performance changes when input size grows.
Identify code that may become a bottleneck.
Choose algorithms that reduce infrastructure cost and improve responsiveness.

sections.title: Understanding Algorithm Growth
sections.content:
Big-O does not measure exact runtime. It measures how quickly work increases as input size increases. The input size is usually represented by n.

If an algorithm checks every element once, its operations grow linearly and its complexity is O(n). If another algorithm repeatedly halves the remaining search area, its operations grow logarithmically and its complexity is O(log n).

The key idea is that growth rate matters more than exact timing when analyzing scalability.

chart.title: Growth rates as input size increases
chart.description: The chart normalizes each curve so beginners can compare the shape of constant, logarithmic, linear, linearithmic, and quadratic growth.

sections.title: Constant Time: O(1)
sections.content:
An algorithm is constant time when the amount of work does not grow as input size increases. The operation may still take real time, but it does not require more steps just because the input contains more items.

Array indexing is the classic example. If the program already knows the index, it can jump directly to that position.

codeSnippets.title: Array indexing uses constant time
codeSnippets.code:
scores = [72, 88, 91, 95, 100]

# Accessing index 3 does not require scanning the whole list.
selected_score = scores[3]
print(selected_score)

sections.title: Linear Time: O(n)
sections.content:
Linear time means the amount of work grows proportionally with input size. If the list doubles, the number of possible checks also roughly doubles.

Linear search demonstrates this behavior because the target might be at the end of the list, or not present at all. In the worst case, the algorithm must inspect every element.

codeSnippets.title: Linear search checks items one by one

sections.title: Logarithmic Time: O(log n)
sections.content:
Logarithmic algorithms reduce the problem size repeatedly. Binary search is the common example: instead of checking every element, it looks at the middle of a sorted list and removes half of the remaining candidates.

For example, a search space can shrink from 16 to 8, then to 4, then to 2, then to 1. This makes logarithmic algorithms highly efficient for large datasets.

codeSnippets.title: Binary search halves the remaining range

sections.title: Quadratic Time: O(n^2)
sections.content:
Quadratic growth often appears when every item is compared with every other item. This is common in simple sorting strategies and pair-comparison problems.

If n is 10, a nested comparison may perform about 100 checks. If n is 1,000, the same pattern may perform about 1,000,000 checks. This rapid multiplication becomes expensive quickly.

codeSnippets.title: Nested loops often multiply the work

sections.title: Comparing Common Complexities
sections.content:
Different Big-O classes describe different growth behaviors. O(1) is constant and is common in array indexing. O(log n) grows very slowly and appears in binary search. O(n) grows linearly and appears in linear search. O(n log n) is common in efficient sorting algorithms such as merge sort. O(n^2) grows rapidly and appears in algorithms such as bubble sort.

This comparison helps developers decide which algorithm is practical for a large-scale system.

subsections.title: Misconception: Big-O measures exact runtime
subsections.content: Big-O measures growth behavior, not exact seconds. Two machines can run the same code at different speeds, but the algorithm's growth pattern remains the same.

subsections.title: Misconception: O(1) means instant
subsections.content: Constant-time operations still take time. O(1) means the amount of work does not grow with input size.

subsections.title: Misconception: The smaller notation is always the best choice
subsections.content: Engineering decisions depend on context. Some solutions trade memory for speed, some are easier to maintain, and some are only faster for large inputs.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: Big-O measures algorithm growth as input size increases.
Efficient algorithms scale better with large datasets.
O(log n) usually grows much more slowly than O(n).
Nested loops often produce O(n^2) behavior.
Complexity analysis helps engineers build scalable software systems.
